claim: Categorization has been associated with distributed networks of the primate brain, including the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC).
source: Categorization has been associated with distributed networks of the primate brain, including the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the context of the manuscript and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Category-selective spiking in PFC and PPC has been established.
source: Although category-selective spiking in PFC and PPC has been established, the frequency-dependent dynamic interactions of frontoparietal networks are largely unexplored.
evidence: This statement references established findings in the field.

claim: The frequency-dependent dynamic interactions of frontoparietal networks are largely unexplored.
source: Although category-selective spiking in PFC and PPC has been established, the frequency-dependent dynamic interactions of frontoparietal networks are largely unexplored.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: Monkeys were trained to perform a delayed-match-to-spatial-category task.
source: We trained monkeys to perform a delayed-match-to-spatial-category task while recording spikes and local field potentials from the PFC and PPC with multiple electrodes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Spikes and local field potentials were recorded from the PFC and PPC with multiple electrodes.
source: We trained monkeys to perform a delayed-match-to-spatial-category task while recording spikes and local field potentials from the PFC and PPC with multiple electrodes.
evidence: This describes the recording methodology used in the study.

claim: Category-selective beta-band synchrony was found between and within the PFC and PPC areas.
source: We found category-selective beta- and delta-band synchrony between and within the areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Category-selective delta-band synchrony was found between and within the PFC and PPC areas.
source: We found category-selective beta- and delta-band synchrony between and within the areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Delta synchrony and spiking activity reflected irrelevant stimulus dimensions in addition to the categories.
source: However, in addition to the categories, delta synchrony and spiking activity also reflected irrelevant stimulus dimensions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Beta synchrony only conveyed information about the task-relevant categories.
source: By contrast, beta synchrony only conveyed information about the task-relevant categories.
evidence: This is a key finding distinguishing beta from delta synchrony based on experimental data.

claim: Category-selective PFC neurons were synchronized with PPC beta oscillations.
source: Further, category-selective PFC neurons were synchronized with PPC beta oscillations, while neurons that carried irrelevant information were not.
evidence: This is a finding from spike-field synchrony analysis.

claim: PFC neurons that carried irrelevant information were not synchronized with PPC beta oscillations.
source: Further, category-selective PFC neurons were synchronized with PPC beta oscillations, while neurons that carried irrelevant information were not.
evidence: This is a finding from spike-field synchrony analysis.

claim: Long-range beta-band synchrony could act as a filter that only supports neural representations of the variables relevant to the task at hand.
source: These results suggest that long-range beta-band synchrony could act as a filter that only supports neural representations of the variables relevant to the task at hand.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, presented as a hypothesis.

claim: Human imaging studies have shown widespread frontal and parietal cortex activation during a broad range of cognitive demands.
source: Human imaging studies have shown widespread frontal and parietal cortex activation during a broad range of cognitive demands (Duncan, 2010; Fedorenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is an intermixing of neurons throughout frontal and parietal cortex that have neural correlates of different cognitive functions including attention, working memory, decision-making, rule-coding, and categorization.
source: Likewise, there is an intermixing of neurons throughout frontal and parietal cortex that have neural correlates of different cognitive functions: attention, working memory, decision-making, rule-coding, and categorization (Andersen and Cui, 2009; Buschman and Miller, 2007; Crowe et al., 2013; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Goodwin et al., 2012; Hayden and Pasternak, 2013; Hussar and Pasternak, 2009; Jacob and Nieder, 2014; Merchant et al., 2011; Rishel et al., 2013; Salazar et al., 2012; Vallentin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The prefrontal and parietal cortices have remarkable similarity in their patterns of neural activity.
source: These two regions not only have remarkable similarity in their patterns of neural activity, but they are also functionally interdependent.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between these brain regions based on established knowledge.

claim: The prefrontal and parietal cortices are functionally interdependent.
source: These two regions not only have remarkable similarity in their patterns of neural activity, but they are also functionally interdependent.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations about deactivation effects.

claim: Deactivating one region (PFC or PPC) decreases neural activity in the other.
source: Deactivating one decreases neural activity in the other (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 2000) and the temporal dynamics of neural information in one can mirror that of the other (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 1998; Crowe et al., 2013; Merchant et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The temporal dynamics of neural information in PFC can mirror that of PPC.
source: Deactivating one decreases neural activity in the other (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 2000) and the temporal dynamics of neural information in one can mirror that of the other (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 1998; Crowe et al., 2013; Merchant et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Understanding executive functions depends on further insight into how the circuits within and between prefrontal and parietal cortices interact.
source: Thus, it is becoming increasingly clear that an understanding of executive functions will depend on further insight into how the circuits within and between prefrontal and parietal cortices interact.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preceding discussion of the literature.

claim: Synchrony in the rhythms of neural activity can reflect network properties.
source: Insight can be gained by examining synchrony in the rhythms of their activity, which can reflect network properties (Miller and Buschman, 2013; Roberts et al., 2013; Thut et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Frequency-dependent increases in frontoparietal synchrony have been seen during shifts of attention.
source: Frequency-dependent increases in their synchrony have been seen during shifts of attention (Buschman and Miller, 2007) and during visual working memory (Salazar et al., 2012), functions long associated with both regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Frequency-dependent increases in frontoparietal synchrony have been seen during visual working memory.
source: Frequency-dependent increases in their synchrony have been seen during shifts of attention (Buschman and Miller, 2007) and during visual working memory (Salazar et al., 2012), functions long associated with both regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Single-neuron studies indicate that both PFC and PPC make a major contribution to visual categorization.
source: More recently, single-neuron studies indicate that both areas also make a major contribution to visual categorization (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2011; Cromer et al., 2010; Crowe et al., 2013; Freedman et al., 2001; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Goodwin et al., 2012; Rishel et al., 2013; Roy et al., 2010; Swaminathan and Freedman, 2012; Tsutsui et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Individual neurons in both PFC and PPC carve up different types of sensory information (motion, shape, location) according to learned category boundaries.
source: Individual neurons in both areas carve up different types of sensory information (i.e., motion, shape, location) according to learned category boundaries.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the cited literature.

claim: The category information carried by neuron spiking in PFC evolves in lock-step with PPC.
source: Further, the category information carried by neuron spiking in one area evolves in lock-step with the other (Crowe et al., 2013; Goodwin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rhythmic synchrony during visual categorization has not been examined prior to this study.
source: Yet, rhythmic synchrony during visual categorization has not been examined.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded from both PFC and PPC while monkeys made decisions about abstract spatial categories.
source: Thus, we recorded local field potentials (LFPs) from both regions while monkeys made decisions about abstract spatial categories.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: A delayed-match-to-category task was used in which monkeys were required to categorize visual cues along an abstract spatial dimension.
source: We used a delayed-match-to-category task in which monkeys were required to categorize visual cues along an abstract spatial dimension and then make a match/non-match decision about whether subsequent test stimuli belonged in the same spatial category as the sample cue.
evidence: This describes the task design used in the study.

claim: Monkeys had to make a match/non-match decision about whether subsequent test stimuli belonged in the same spatial category as the sample cue.
source: We used a delayed-match-to-category task in which monkeys were required to categorize visual cues along an abstract spatial dimension and then make a match/non-match decision about whether subsequent test stimuli belonged in the same spatial category as the sample cue.
evidence: This describes the task requirements.

claim: Match/non-match category decision tasks have been shown to engage PFC and PPC neurons.
source: This type of match/non-match category decision has been shown to engage PFC and PPC neurons (Cromer et al., 2010; Crowe et al., 2013; Freedman et al., 2001; Goodwin et al., 2012; Roy et al., 2010; Swaminathan and Freedman, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increases in synchrony between and within frontoparietal networks were found that depended on whether monkeys categorized a stimulus as 'Above' or 'Below'.
source: We found increases in synchrony between and within frontoparietal networks that depended on whether monkeys categorized a stimulus as 'Above' or 'Below'.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Spiking activity that reflected the category distinction was better synchronized to frontoparietal LFP category networks than spiking that encoded task-irrelevant information.
source: Moreover, we found that spiking activity that reflected the category distinction was better synchronized to frontoparietal LFP category networks than spiking that encoded information irrelevant to the task.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on spike-field synchrony analysis.

claim: Two rhesus macaque monkeys were trained to perform a Go/No-go category matching task.
source: Two rhesus macaque monkeys were trained to perform a Go/No-go category matching task.
evidence: This describes the subjects and task used in the study.

claim: The trial began when monkeys held a bar and achieved fixation of a central target.
source: The trial began when they held a bar and achieved fixation of a central target (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the task procedure, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The initial Above vs. Below category boundaries were indicated by two horizontal lines on each side of fixation.
source: The initial Above vs. Below category boundaries were indicated by two horizontal lines on each side of fixation, which divided the top from bottom halves of the screen.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: A sample cue appeared briefly at a location chosen randomly from a set of 16 locations on the right or left side of the screen.
source: After the monkeys initiated the trial, the boundaries disappeared and a sample cue appeared briefly at a location chosen randomly from a set of 16 locations (± a small jitter) on the right or left side of the screen (Figure 1B; 144 possible locations in total).
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: There were 144 possible sample locations in total.
source: After the monkeys initiated the trial, the boundaries disappeared and a sample cue appeared briefly at a location chosen randomly from a set of 16 locations (± a small jitter) on the right or left side of the screen (Figure 1B; 144 possible locations in total).
evidence: This describes the stimulus space, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: After a 500 ms post-sample delay, the two horizontal lines reappeared at shifted positions.
source: After a 500 ms post-sample delay, the two horizontal lines reappeared at shifted positions.
evidence: This describes the task timing and procedure.

claim: On half of the trials, the boundary lines shifted clockwise (the left shifted up and the right shifted down by 4 degrees).
source: On half of the trials, the lines shifted clockwise (the left shifted up and the right shifted down by 4 degrees).
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: On half of the trials, the boundary lines shifted counter clockwise.
source: On the other half of the trials, they shifted counter clockwise (the opposite).
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: After an additional 1 s delay, a test stimulus appeared randomly at one of 624 possible locations.
source: After an additional 1 s delay, a test stimulus appeared randomly at one of 624 possible locations (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the task procedure, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The test stimulus was a category match if it appeared on the same side of the shifted horizontal line as the sample had appeared relative to the original horizontal line.
source: This test stimulus was a category match if it appeared on the same side of the (shifted) horizontal line (Above or Below) as the sample had appeared relative to the original horizontal line, irrespective of its exact location.
evidence: This describes the task rule.

claim: If the test stimulus was a match, the monkey had to release the bar within 1 s to receive a juice reward.
source: If the test stimulus was a match, the monkey had to release the bar within 1 s (Go) to receive a juice reward.
evidence: This describes the task requirements and reward contingency.

claim: If the test was a non-match, the animals continued holding the bar until another test stimulus (always a match) appeared on the screen.
source: If the test was a non-match, the animals continued holding the bar (No-go) until another test stimulus (always a match) appeared on the screen.
evidence: This describes the task requirements.

claim: The category of the initial sample cue did not change with the boundary shift.
source: Note that the category of the initial sample cue did not change with the boundary shift.
evidence: This clarifies an important aspect of the task design.

claim: The boundary shift only changed which test stimulus locations would qualify as a category match or non-match.
source: The boundary shift only changed which test stimulus locations would qualify as a category match or non-match.
evidence: This clarifies the purpose of the boundary shift in the task design.

claim: The purpose of the boundary shift was to ensure that the monkeys were encoding an abstract category representation, not solely based on retinotopic coordinates.
source: Thus, the purpose of the boundary shift was to ensure that the monkeys were encoding an abstract category representation, one that was not solely based on retinotopic coordinates.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the task design.

claim: The monkeys could not make a decision based solely on the proximity between sample and test stimuli because they could often be quite far apart yet still belong to the same category.
source: The monkeys also could not make a decision based solely on the proximity between sample and test stimuli because they could often be quite far apart (e.g., on the right and left of the screen; see Figure 1A), yet still belong to the same category.
evidence: This explains another aspect of the task design that requires abstract categorization.

claim: Both monkeys performed the task quite well, with 92.77% of all trials (excluding fixation breaks) correct.
source: Both monkeys performed the task quite well, with 92.77% of all trials (excluding fixation breaks) correct.
evidence: This reports the behavioral performance data.

claim: PABOVE was at least 0.83 if the sample was Above and at most 0.13 if the sample was Below.
source: Overall, PABOVE was at least 0.83 if the sample was also Above (above the horizontal meridian) and at most 0.13 if the sample was actually Below.
evidence: This quantifies the monkeys' categorization behavior based on data analysis.

claim: The probability of the monkeys categorizing the sample as Left ranged from 0.39 to 0.57.
source: Thus, just as we did for Above vs. Below, we computed the probability of the monkeys categorizing the sample as Left. This ranged from 0.39 to 0.57 (Figure 1C), which is what we would expect if the monkeys were disregarding Left vs. Right (irrelevant dimension) and categorizing by Above vs. Below (relevant dimension).
evidence: This quantifies the monkeys' behavior on the irrelevant dimension, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The monkeys were generalizing across diverse locations within the same category and not mistakenly categorizing the sample and test as being in different categories simply because they were far apart.
source: Thus, the monkeys were generalizing across diverse locations within the same category and not mistakenly categorizing the sample and test as being in different categories simply because they were far apart.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Above vs. Below category performance remained high (at least 85% correct) regardless of sample cue eccentricity, sample distance from the horizontal and vertical meridians, the visual quadrant or hemifield of sample display, and the distance between the sample and test stimuli.
source: Likewise, Above vs. Below category performance remained high (at least 85% correct), regardless of sample cue eccentricity, sample distance from the horizontal and vertical meridians, the visual quadrant or hemifield of sample display, and the distance between the sample and test stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data across various conditions, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Performance remained high (at least 85% correct) on trials in which the retinotopic location that was occupied by the sample stimulus changed categories after the shift in boundaries.
source: Finally, performance remained high (at least 85% correct) on trials in which the retinotopic location that was occupied by the sample stimulus changed categories after the shift in boundaries and that location became a category non-match (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data for a specific trial type, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The monkeys' behavior showed the hallmark of categorization: sharp discrimination across the boundary and flat generalization on either side of a boundary.
source: Thus, the monkeys' behavior showed the hallmark of categorization: sharp discrimination across the boundary and flat generalization on either side of a boundary.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: The monkeys maintained a category representation that was uncoupled from the particular spatial location of the sample stimulus.
source: The monkeys maintained a category representation that was uncoupled from the particular spatial location of the sample stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Recordings were made from the lateral PFC (lPFC, areas 46 and 45), caudal PFC (cPFC, area 8A and the FEF), and the anterior intraparietal area (AIP).
source: We recorded from multiple electrodes simultaneously advanced in the lateral PFC (lPFC, areas 46 and 45), caudal PFC (cPFC, area 8A and the FEF), and the anterior intraparietal area (AIP; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the recording locations, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AIP subregion of the posterior parietal cortex was selected because it is strongly coupled to premotor areas and plays a role in visuospatial transformations that guide motor movements.
source: The AIP subregion of the posterior parietal cortex was selected because it is strongly coupled to premotor areas and plays a role in visuospatial transformations that guide motor movements (Verhoef et al., 2015).
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting AIP, supported by a citation.

claim: Data from subareas of the lPFC were combined because they yielded similar results.
source: Data from subareas of the lPFC (as well as subareas of the cPFC) were combined because they yielded similar results.
evidence: This explains a data analysis decision based on observed similarity.

claim: LFPs were recorded from a total of 159 electrodes in AIP, 111 electrodes in cPFC, and 129 electrodes in lPFC.
source: To examine interactions between the areas, we analyzed simultaneously recorded LFPs from a total of 159 electrodes in AIP, 111 electrodes in cPFC, and 129 electrodes in lPFC.
evidence: This reports the number of recording sites used in the analysis.

claim: Stimulus-evoked components were removed from the LFP to isolate the task-induced oscillations.
source: From the LFP we first removed stimulus-evoked components (to isolate the task-induced oscillations), and decomposed it in the frequency domain using the Morlet wavelet.
evidence: This describes a data processing step.

claim: The LFP was decomposed in six octaves (from 2–128 Hz), at a resolution of 0.1 octave.
source: The LFP was decomposed in six octaves (from 2–128 Hz), at a resolution of 0.1 octave.
evidence: This describes the frequency analysis parameters.

claim: LFP power was normalized to 1/frequency to correct the power-law decay of the LFP power spectrum.
source: From the amplitude of the wave components we then computed the LFP time- and frequency-dependent power and normalized it to 1/frequency (in order to correct the power-law decay of the LFP power spectrum).
evidence: This describes a data normalization procedure.

claim: Removing the LFP components that are phase-locked to the stimulus may conceal high-frequency rhythms time-locked to stimulus presentation, but it is necessary to avoid spurious synchrony due to simultaneous stimulus-evoked responses in the LFPs.
source: Removing the LFP components that are phase-locked to the stimulus may conceal high-frequency rhythms time-locked to stimulus presentation, but it is necessary to avoid spurious synchrony due to simultaneous stimulus-evoked responses in the LFPs.
evidence: This explains the rationale for a data processing decision.

claim: Elevated power of the 16–32 Hz octave (beta band) was revealed in all three areas.
source: This analysis revealed elevated power of the 16–32 Hz octave (beta band) in all three areas (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral analysis, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Beta-band power was especially prominent at the end of the sample presentation and in the early part of the immediately following delay.
source: Beta-band power was especially prominent at the end of the sample presentation and in the early part of the immediately following delay.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of beta power based on data analysis.

claim: The time when beta power was prominent is around the time that the monkey would be expected to categorize the location of the sample.
source: This is around the time that we would expect the monkey to categorize the location of the sample.
evidence: This is an inference about the cognitive process based on task timing.

claim: Beta power was also evident just before presentation of the test stimulus, after the boundaries switched.
source: Beta power was also evident just before presentation of the test stimulus, after the boundaries switched.
evidence: This describes another temporal feature of beta power based on data analysis.

claim: There was significantly greater beta power during the Category epoch (average: 0.06 mV2 ± SEM: 0.002) than the Shift epoch (0.04 ± 0.002; p=4.7×10–10).
source: As suggested by Figure 2A, there was significantly greater power during the Category epoch (average: 0.06 mV2 ± SEM: 0.002) than the Shift epoch (0.04 ± 0.002; p=4.7×10–10).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison of beta power across epochs.

claim: The strongest beta power appeared in AIP, followed by cPFC.
source: The strongest beta power appeared in AIP, followed by cPFC (p=3.4×10−23; posthoc comparisons: AIP (0.065 ± 0.002) > cPFC (0.05 ± 0.002), p=7×10–10; cPFC > lPFC (0.03 ± 0.002), p=2.6×10–3; AIP>lPFC, p=4.7×10–12).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison of beta power across brain areas.

claim: Beta band synchrony was evident within the areas (AIP-AIP, cPFC-cPFC, lPFC-lPFC).
source: The pattern of synchrony largely paralleled the spectral power results. Beta band synchrony was evident within the areas (Figure 2B; AIP-AIP: n = 340 pairs of electrodes; cPFC-cPFC: n = 205 pairs; lPFC-lPFC: n = 290 pairs) and between areas (Figure 2C; AIP-cPFC: n = 474 pairs; cPFC-lPFC: n = 323 pairs; AIP-lPFC: n = 535 pairs).
evidence: This reports synchrony findings, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Beta band synchrony was evident between areas (AIP-cPFC, cPFC-lPFC, AIP-lPFC).
source: The pattern of synchrony largely paralleled the spectral power results. Beta band synchrony was evident within the areas (Figure 2B; AIP-AIP: n = 340 pairs of electrodes; cPFC-cPFC: n = 205 pairs; lPFC-lPFC: n = 290 pairs) and between areas (Figure 2C; AIP-cPFC: n = 474 pairs; cPFC-lPFC: n = 323 pairs; AIP-lPFC: n = 535 pairs).
evidence: This reports synchrony findings, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: There was significantly greater beta synchrony in the Category epoch (0.09 ± 0.002) than the Shift epoch (0.07 ± 0.002; p=2.7×10–10).
source: Like the power analysis, there was significantly greater beta synchrony in the Category epoch (0.09 ± 0.002) than the Shift epoch (0.07 ± 0.002; p=2.7×10–10).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison of beta synchrony across epochs.

claim: The strongest beta synchrony was within AIP and weakest between AIP and lPFC.
source: The strongest was within AIP and weakest between AIP and lPFC. (Posthoc comparisons, corrected p<0.01: AIP-AIP (0.18 ± 0.003) > cPFC-cPFC (0.13 ± 0.004) > lPFC-lPFC (0.08 ± 0.003) > cPFC-lPFC (0.04 ± 0.003) > AIP-lPFC (0.02 ± 0.003); AIP-cPFC (0.03 ± 0.003) not different from AIP-lPFC and cPFC-lPFC).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison of beta synchrony across area pairs.

claim: The low-frequency synchrony observed late in the trial during the test stimulus may be related to the motor response to a category match, the reward that followed correct trials, or the eye movement that typically follows the release from visual fixation requirement.
source: The low-frequency synchrony that was observed late in the trial, during the test stimulus (Figure 2B and C), may be related to the motor response to a category match (in 50% of the trials), the reward that followed correct trials, or the eye movement that typically follows the release from visual fixation requirement.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the late-trial synchrony, with reference to Figures 2B and C.

claim: Previous studies have shown rule and category-selective beta synchrony within the PFC and between the PFC and striatum.
source: Previous studies have shown rule and category-selective beta synchrony within the PFC and between the PFC and striatum (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2014; Buschman et al., 2012), wherein different pairs of electrodes showed increased beta synchrony for one or the other category/rule.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Different pairs of electrodes showed increased beta synchrony for one or the other category in previous studies.
source: Previous studies have shown rule and category-selective beta synchrony within the PFC and between the PFC and striatum (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2014; Buschman et al., 2012), wherein different pairs of electrodes showed increased beta synchrony for one or the other category/rule.
evidence: This describes findings from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The same pattern of category-selective beta synchrony was found for frontoparietal synchrony and spatial categories in the current study.
source: We found the same results for frontoparietal synchrony and spatial categories.
evidence: This states that the current findings replicate prior patterns in a new context.

claim: A cPFC electrode had stronger beta synchrony with one AIP electrode for Above but stronger beta synchrony with another AIP electrode for Below.
source: The cPFC (F09) electrode had stronger beta synchrony with one AIP electrode (P07) for Above (red and black traces, left) but stronger beta synchrony with the other AIP electrode (P10) for Below (red and green traces, right).
evidence: This describes an example of category-selective synchrony shown in Figure 3.

claim: Category-selective synchrony for Above/Below categories was found both between and within the areas, predominantly in beta (16–32 Hz) and delta (2–4 Hz) bands.
source: This revealed category-selective synchrony for Above/Below categories both between and within the areas (Figure 4A and C respectively), predominantly in two octaves: 16–32 Hz (beta), and 2–4 Hz (delta).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the synchrony analysis, with reference to Figure 4A and C.

claim: Category selective synchrony between AIP and cPFC was mostly concentrated in the beta band during the Category epoch and in the delta band during the Shift epoch.
source: Category-selective synchrony between AIP and cPFC was mostly concentrated in the beta band during the Category epoch and in the delta band during the Shift epoch (Figure 4A left panel).
evidence: This describes the temporal and spectral characteristics of category-selective synchrony, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Category selective synchrony between cPFC and lPFC electrodes was similar to that between AIP and cPFC.
source: Category selective synchrony between cPFC and lPFC electrodes (Figure 4A middle panel) was similar.
evidence: This compares synchrony patterns across area pairs, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: lPFC and AIP category selective synchrony was mostly in the low-frequency oscillations.
source: By contrast, lPFC and AIP category selective synchrony was mostly in the low-frequency oscillations (Figure 4A right panel).
evidence: This describes a difference in synchrony patterns for this area pair, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Within AIP, category-selective synchrony was longer-lasting and covered a wider range of frequencies.
source: Within AIP, category-selective synchrony was longer-lasting and covered a wider range of frequencies (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of within-area synchrony in AIP, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The observed category-selective synchrony did not arise from a difference in the pattern of network dynamics between the categories.
source: In addition, the observed category-selective synchrony did not arise from a difference in the pattern of network dynamics between the categories. Both the synchrony between and within the frontal and parietal areas displayed similar time-frequency dependence for the category Above as for the Below (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This rules out an alternative explanation for the findings, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both beta and delta rhythms displayed synchrony that was significantly selective for Above vs. Below.
source: As seen at the upper half of Figure 5, both beta and delta rhythms displayed synchrony that was significantly selective for Above vs. Below (i.e., the corrected 95% CIs were greater than zero).
evidence: This reports a statistical finding from the ANOVA analysis, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: None of the area combinations showed beta synchrony selective for Right vs. Left.
source: None of the area combinations showed beta synchrony selective for Right vs. Left (bottom quadrant of Figure 5).
evidence: This reports a negative finding for beta synchrony on the irrelevant dimension, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Delta synchrony was not selective for Right vs. Left within any area but was selective in the cross-area interactions and only during the Shift epoch.
source: Delta synchrony was not selective for Right vs. Left within any area but was selective in the cross-area interactions (i.e., AIP-cPFC, cPFC-lPFC, and AIP-lPFC) and only during the Shift epoch.
evidence: This describes the specificity of delta synchrony for the irrelevant dimension.

claim: Pure category-selective synchrony was restricted to the beta band.
source: Thus, pure category-selective synchrony was restricted to the beta band.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of beta and delta synchrony patterns.

claim: There was more delta selectivity for Above vs. Below but also some delta selectivity for Right vs. Left.
source: There was more delta selectivity for Above vs. Below but also some delta selectivity for Right vs. Left.
evidence: This summarizes the delta synchrony findings.

claim: 1078 single neurons were isolated from the electrodes (296 from cPFC, 387 from lPFC, and 395 from AIP).
source: From the same electrodes we isolated the spiking activity of 1078 single neurons (296 from cPFC, 387 from lPFC, and 395 from AIP).
evidence: This reports the number of neurons recorded from each area.

claim: Spiking activity in PFC and PPC showed selectivity for the learned spatial categories (Above vs. Below).
source: As previously reported (Goodwin et al., 2012), spiking activity in these areas showed selectivity for the learned spatial categories (Above vs. Below).
evidence: This finding replicates prior research, supported by a citation.

claim: Selectivity for the Above vs. Below categories was evident shortly after the onset of the sample cue and continued throughout the remainder of the trial, growing stronger in the delay following the sample.
source: Note that selectivity for the Above vs. Below categories was evident shortly after the onset of the sample cue and continued throughout the remainder of the trial, growing stronger in the delay following the sample.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of category selectivity in spiking activity based on data analysis.

claim: Category selectivity in spiking activity was strongest in cPFC, next in lPFC, and weakest in AIP.
source: This figure also shows that category selectivity in spiking activity was strongest in cPFC, next in lPFC, and weakest in AIP (effect of area from 2-way ANOVA: p=7.9×10–22; post-hoc comparisons with corrected p<0.05: cPFC (1.24 ± 0.07) > lPFC (0.62 ± 0.06) > AIP (0.39 ± 0.06)).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison of category selectivity across brain areas.

claim: Beta band was of particular interest because beta oscillations have been associated with a variety of cognitive functions.
source: For our LFP analyses (discussed above), the beta band was of particular interest because beta oscillations have been associated with a variety of cognitive functions and previous studies have shown category and rule selectivity in this band (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2014; Buschman et al., 2012).
evidence: This explains the rationale for focusing on beta band, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have shown category and rule selectivity in the beta band.
source: For our LFP analyses (discussed above), the beta band was of particular interest because beta oscillations have been associated with a variety of cognitive functions and previous studies have shown category and rule selectivity in this band (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2014; Buschman et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There was category-selective beta-band synchrony within and between each area.
source: As noted above, there was category-selective beta-band synchrony within and between each area.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding from the synchrony analysis.

claim: There was virtually no selective beta synchrony for the task-irrelevant Right vs. Left hemifield location of the sample cue.
source: However, there was virtually no selective beta synchrony for the (task-irrelevant) Right vs. Left hemifield location of the sample cue.
evidence: This reports a negative finding for beta synchrony on the irrelevant dimension.

claim: The spiking of single neurons was sensitive to the Right vs. Left location of the sample.
source: By contrast, the spiking of single neurons was sensitive to the Right vs. Left location of the sample. This is shown in Figure 6C and D.
evidence: This reports a finding from spiking analysis, with reference to Figure 6C and D.

claim: The average population activity of all three areas showed significant selectivity for Right vs. Left early on during sample display, albeit weaker than the learned Above vs. Below categories.
source: The average population activity of all three areas showed significant selectivity for Right vs. Left early on during sample display, albeit weaker than the learned Above vs. Below categories.
evidence: This reports a finding from population spiking analysis.

claim: Right vs. Left selectivity was strongest in the prefrontal cortex (cPFC and lPFC) and weak in AIP.
source: Right vs. Left selectivity was strongest in the prefrontal cortex (cPFC and lPFC) and weak in AIP (effect of area from 2-way ANOVA: p=3.1×10–8; post-hoc comparisons with corrected p<0.05: AIP (0.1 ± 0.02) < cPFC (0.22 ± 0.02) and lPFC (0.27 ± 0.02), cPFC not different from lPFC).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison of Right/Left selectivity across brain areas.

claim: Information about the task-irrelevant Right vs. Left location of the sample 'leaked through' in spiking activity but did not seem to do so for the beta synchrony.
source: Thus, information about the task-irrelevant Right vs. Left location of the sample 'leaked through' in spiking activity but did not seem to do so for the beta synchrony (but, as noted, did for the delta synchrony).
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the selectivity patterns in spiking vs. synchrony.

claim: Beta power and synchrony was strongest within AIP and between AIP and the other areas.
source: As noted above, beta power and synchrony was strongest within AIP and between AIP and the other areas.
evidence: This summarizes a finding about the distribution of beta activity across areas.

claim: Beta category-selectivity was strongest within AIP.
source: Beta category-selectivity was also strongest within AIP.
evidence: This reports a finding about category selectivity in beta synchrony.

claim: AIP showed the weakest category selectivity in the spiking rate of its neurons.
source: However, as Figure 6 shows, AIP showed the weakest category selectivity in the spiking rate of its neurons.
evidence: This reports a finding about spiking selectivity, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The difference in category selectivity strength between AIP and other areas is not because there were fewer isolated neurons in AIP vs. other areas.
source: This is not because there were fewer isolated neurons in AIP vs. other areas (see above for numbers of neurons from each area).
evidence: This rules out a potential confound in the comparison.

claim: The average number of isolated neurons per electrode was similar across areas (AIP: 2.48 neurons/electrode; cPFC: 2.67; lPFC: 3).
source: The average number of isolated neurons per electrode was also similar across areas (AIP: 2.48 neurons/electrode; cPFC: 2.67; lPFC: 3; note that electrodes with zero neurons were not included in any of the LFP analyses).
evidence: This reports a control analysis to rule out sampling bias.

claim: LFP synchrony displayed similar dynamics between pairs of electrodes that had the same category preference in their spiking activity as those that had different category preferences.
source: LFP synchrony displayed similar dynamics between pairs of electrodes that had the same category preference in their spiking activity as those that had different category preferences (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This reports a finding about the relationship between spiking and LFP synchrony, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Synchrony between spikes in area A and LFPs in area B, but not the other way around, may suggest a unidirectional influence from A to B.
source: Synchrony between spikes in area A (the neuronal output from A) and LFPs in area B (presumably reflecting the synaptic inputs to B), but not the other way around, may suggest a unidirectional influence from A to B.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of asymmetric spike-field synchrony.

claim: Significant spike-LFP synchrony was found between cPFC spikes and AIP LFP beta oscillations.
source: This analysis revealed significant spike-LFP synchrony between cPFC spikes and AIP LFP beta oscillations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the spike-field analysis.

claim: cPFC spikes tended to appear at the downstroke of the AIP LFP cycle.
source: As the superposition indicates, the cPFC spikes tended to appear at the same phase of the LFP oscillation, namely the downstroke of the LFP cycle.
evidence: This describes the phase relationship observed in the example shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was significantly stronger phase-coupling of cPFC spikes to AIP LFP oscillations in the 22–32 Hz band (0.006 ± 0.002) than the other way around (−0.001 ± 0.001; t-test: p=0.004).
source: This synchrony was asymmetric: there was significantly stronger phase-coupling of cPFC spikes to AIP LFP oscillations in the 22–32 Hz band (0.006 ± 0.002) than the other way around (−0.001 ± 0.001; phase-coupling of cPFC oscillations to AIP spikes, t-test: p=0.004).
evidence: This reports a statistical finding demonstrating asymmetric spike-field synchrony.

claim: The asymmetry in cPFC-AIP spike-LFP synchrony was more pronounced for the category Below than Above.
source: This asymmetry was more pronounced for the category Below than Above (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports a category-specific difference in the asymmetry, with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No frequency-dependent spike-LFP synchrony was observed between lPFC spikes and AIP LFPs or the reverse.
source: No frequency-dependent spike-LFP synchrony was observed between lPFC spikes and AIP LFPs or the reverse (Figure 7C).
evidence: This reports a negative finding for this area pair, with reference to Figure 7C.

claim: There was only modest synchrony between cPFC spikes and lPFC LFPs in the beta band, but this was not significantly unidirectional.
source: There was only modest synchrony between cPFC spikes and lPFC LFPs in the beta band, but this was not significantly unidirectional (Figure 7D).
evidence: This reports a finding for this area pair, with reference to Figure 7D.

claim: The pairs of frontoparietal sites that displayed category-selective beta synchrony also showed strong spike-LFP synchrony in the beta band.
source: These results indicate that the pairs of frontoparietal sites that displayed category-selective beta synchrony also showed strong spike-LFP synchrony in the beta band.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between LFP-LFP and spike-LFP synchrony.

claim: Pairs of frontoparietal sites that displayed strong spike-LFP synchrony displayed more pronounced category-selective synchrony of beta rhythms.
source: Conversely, pairs of frontoparietal sites that displayed strong spike-LFP synchrony displayed more pronounced category-selective synchrony of beta rhythms (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports a finding about the relationship between spike-LFP and LFP-LFP synchrony, with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: cPFC electrodes with spiking selectivity for the relevant category distinction (Above vs. Below) showed stronger synchrony with AIP beta oscillations than the cPFC electrodes with spiking selectivity for the irrelevant dimension (Right vs. Left).
source: Indeed, we found that cPFC electrodes with spiking selectivity for the relevant category distinction (Above vs. Below) showed stronger synchrony with AIP beta oscillations than the cPFC electrodes with spiking selectivity for the irrelevant dimension (Right vs. Left).
evidence: This is a key finding showing that task-relevant spiking is preferentially synchronized.

claim: Synchrony of AIP LFPs with cPFC spikes that had Above/Below selectivity (n = 54 spike-LFP pairs, 0.01 ± 0.002) was significantly different from zero (t-test comparison to zero, p=1.7×10–6).
source: In fact, synchrony of cPFC spikes to AIP LFPs was significant for spikes with Above/Below selectivity (n = 54 spike-LFP pairs, 0.01 ± 0.002, t-test comparison to zero, p=1.7×10–6), but not different from zero for spikes with Right/Left selectivity (n = 44 spike-LFP pairs, −0.003 ± 0.002, p=0.98).
evidence: This reports a statistical test of spike-field synchrony for task-relevant spikes.

claim: Synchrony of cPFC spikes to AIP LFPs was not different from zero for spikes with Right/Left selectivity (n = 44 spike-LFP pairs, −0.003 ± 0.002, p=0.98).
source: In fact, synchrony of cPFC spikes to AIP LFPs was significant for spikes with Above/Below selectivity (n = 54 spike-LFP pairs, 0.01 ± 0.002, t-test comparison to zero, p=1.7×10–6), but not different from zero for spikes with Right/Left selectivity (n = 44 spike-LFP pairs, −0.003 ± 0.002, p=0.98).
evidence: This reports a statistical test showing no spike-field synchrony for task-irrelevant spikes.

claim: Synchrony between AIP spikes and cPFC LFPs was significant for both Above/Below and Right/Left selective spikes, with no difference between them.
source: By contrast, synchrony between AIP spikes and cPFC LFPs was significant (Figure 8B; Above/Below: n = 50, 0.006 ± 0.002, p=3.7×10–4; Right vs. Left: n = 52, 0.004 ± 0.001, p=0.001) but there was no difference between AIP spikes with Above/Below vs. Right/Left selectivity (p=0.32).
evidence: This reports a finding showing no selectivity in the reverse direction, with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: There was little or no cPFC-AIP spike-LFP synchrony in the Shift epoch for either Above/Below or Right/Left selective spikes.
source: By contrast, there was little or no cPFC-AIP spike-LFP synchrony in the Shift epoch for either Above/Below or Right/Left selective spikes (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This reports a negative finding for the Shift epoch, with reference to Figure 8C,D.

claim: There was only modest spike-LFP synchrony between lPFC and AIP, or between cPFC and lPFC, in either direction, regardless of Above/Below or Right/Left selectivity.
source: Finally, there was only modest spike-LFP synchrony between lPFC and AIP, or between cPFC and lPFC, in either direction, regardless of Above/Below or Right/Left selectivity (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports negative findings for other area pairs, with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was significant linear correlation between the Above/Below spike rate selectivity of cPFC electrodes and their synchrony to the AIP beta rhythms (Pearson's r=0.25, p=0.009).
source: Indeed, as Figure 9 illustrates, there was significant linear (but not rank) correlation between the Above/Below spike rate selectivity of cPFC electrodes and their synchrony to the AIP beta rhythms (averaged across all simultaneously recorded AIP electrodes: Pearson's r=0.25, p=0.009; Spearman's rank r=0.16, p=0.09).
evidence: This reports a correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claim: There was no linear or rank correlation between the Right/Left spike rate selectivity of cPFC electrodes and their synchrony to parietal beta rhythms (Pearson's r=−0.11, p=0.28; Spearman's rank r=−0.04, p=0.70).
source: By contrast, there was no linear (or rank) correlation between the Right/Left spike rate selectivity of the same cPFC electrodes and their synchrony to parietal beta rhythms (Pearson's r=−0.11, p=0.28; Spearman's rank r=−0.04, p=0.70).
evidence: This reports a negative correlation result for the irrelevant dimension.

claim: During a rule-based spatial categorization task, there was an increase in beta-band oscillatory power and synchrony within and between the prefrontal cortex and parietal cortex.
source: We found that during a rule-based spatial categorization task, there was an increase in beta-band oscillatory power and synchrony within and between the prefrontal cortex and parietal cortex.
evidence: This summarizes a primary finding of the study.

claim: Different pairs of recording sites, both within and between the prefrontal cortex and parietal cortex, showed category selectivity (increased LFP synchrony for one or the other category), primarily in the beta but also in the delta band.
source: Different pairs of recording sites, both within and between the prefrontal cortex and parietal cortex, showed category selectivity, that is, increased LFP synchrony for one or the other category, primarily in the beta but also in the delta band.
evidence: This summarizes a primary finding of the study.

claim: Each category was accompanied by different network patterns of synchrony.
source: Thus, each category was accompanied by different network patterns of synchrony.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the category-selective synchrony findings.

claim: Prefrontal spikes were synchronized to parietal LFP beta rhythms, but parietal spikes were not synchronized to prefrontal rhythms.
source: Prefrontal spikes were synchronized to parietal LFP beta rhythms, but parietal spikes were not synchronized to prefrontal rhythms.
evidence: This summarizes the asymmetric spike-field synchrony finding.

claim: The asymmetric spike-field synchrony suggests a unidirectional influence with the PFC influencing the parietal cortex.
source: This suggests a unidirectional influence with the PFC influencing the parietal cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the asymmetric synchrony finding.

claim: Prefrontal neural spiking selective for the task-relevant Above vs. Below category dimension was synchronized with the parietal beta rhythms, but spiking that reflected the task-irrelevant Right vs Left dimension was not.
source: Finally, we found that prefrontal neural spiking selective for the task-relevant Above vs. Below category dimension was synchronized with the parietal beta rhythms, but spiking that reflected the task-irrelevant Right vs Left dimension was not.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about selective synchronization of task-relevant information.

claim: Oscillatory synchrony has been suggested to play a role in establishing functional networks.
source: Oscillatory synchrony has been suggested to play a role in establishing functional networks (Engel et al., 2001; Fries, 2005; Miller and Buschman, 2013; Uhlhaas et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The finding of category-selective patterns of increased synchrony between recording sites in the frontoparietal cortex supports the idea that oscillatory synchrony plays a role in establishing functional networks.
source: Our finding of category-selective patterns of increased synchrony between recording sites in the frontoparietal cortex supports this.
evidence: This connects the current findings to the broader theoretical framework.

claim: There is object-selective synchrony between the prefrontal and parietal cortex for different objects held in working memory.
source: For example, there is object-selective synchrony between the prefrontal and parietal cortex for different objects held in working memory (Salazar et al., 2012) and within the prefrontal cortex for different behavioral rules (Buschman et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There is rule-selective synchrony within the prefrontal cortex for different behavioral rules.
source: For example, there is object-selective synchrony between the prefrontal and parietal cortex for different objects held in working memory (Salazar et al., 2012) and within the prefrontal cortex for different behavioral rules (Buschman et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Category-selective patterns of synchrony develop between the prefrontal cortex and striatum in parallel with category learning.
source: Further, category-selective patterns of synchrony develop between the prefrontal cortex and striatum in parallel with category learning (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Selective synchrony of gamma rhythms between V4 and V1 has been reported to guide attentional selection in primates.
source: Selective synchrony of gamma rhythms between V4 and V1 has been reported to guide attentional selection in primates (Bosman et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A recent study in humans suggests functional networks across the cortex are formed by harmonic patterns constrained by known anatomy.
source: A recent study in humans suggests functional networks across the cortex are formed by harmonic patterns constrained by known anatomy (Atasoy et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Anatomy (the connectome) may be the infrastructure that determines which functional circuits can potentially form.
source: In other words, it seems as if anatomy (the connectome) may be the infrastructure that determines which functional circuits can potentially form.
evidence: This is an interpretation synthesizing findings from the literature.

claim: Which circuits form from moment to moment may be regulated, at least in part, by patterns of synchrony.
source: Which circuits do form from moment to moment may be regulated, at least in part, by patterns of synchrony.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of synchrony.

claim: Rhythmic ensembles tend to center on the beta band.
source: In prior reports, as well as in this study, these 'rhythmic ensembles' tend to center on the beta band (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2014; Buschman et al., 2012; Haegens et al., 2011; Micheli et al., 2015; Salazar et al., 2012; Siegel et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and the current findings.

claim: There is increasing evidence that beta-band synchrony may play a role in sustained top-down, or feedback, signaling in the cortex.
source: This is noteworthy because there is increasing evidence that beta-band synchrony may play a role in sustained top-down, or feedback, signaling in the cortex (Bastos et al., 2015; Engel and Fries, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Category selectivity was more 'pure' in synchrony (especially in the beta band) than for spiking activity.
source: In line with this is our observation that category selectivity was more 'pure' in synchrony (especially in the beta band) than for spiking activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the selectivity patterns in synchrony vs. spiking.

claim: Beta synchrony was selective for the task relevant categories, but no (irrelevant) information about the left vs. right hemifield location of the sample cue could be detected in beta synchrony.
source: While beta synchrony was selective for the task relevant categories, we could not detect any (irrelevant) information about the left vs. right hemifield location of the sample cue in beta synchrony.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about the selectivity of beta synchrony.

claim: Left vs. right hemifield information was detectable in neural spike rates.
source: By contrast, left vs. right was detectable in neural spike rates.
evidence: This contrasts the selectivity in spiking vs. synchrony.

claim: The difference in selectivity between spiking rate and LFP synchrony could merely reflect differences in the ability to detect information in them.
source: Of course, selectivity of spiking rate and LFP synchrony are two different phenomena, which rely on different measures and analyses. Thus, this difference could merely reflect differences in the ability to detect information in them.
evidence: This acknowledges a potential alternative explanation for the observed difference.

claim: It is possible that beta synchrony is more selective than spiking activity.
source: But it is also possible that beta synchrony is more selective.
evidence: This presents an alternative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Beta synchrony may provide an additional level of filtering beyond that seen in spiking activity.
source: Beta synchrony may provide an additional level of filtering beyond that seen in spiking activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of beta synchrony.

claim: Because of its putative role in feedback processing in the cortex, beta synchrony may only pass back top-down information to other cortical areas.
source: Because of its putative role in feedback processing in the cortex, it may only pass back top-down information to other cortical areas.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of beta synchrony based on its proposed role in feedback.

claim: Only the prefrontal spiking activity that conveyed task-relevant information was synchronized to the parietal beta rhythms.
source: Support for this also comes from our finding that only the prefrontal spiking activity that conveyed task-relevant information was synchronized to the parietal beta rhythms.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding supporting the filtering hypothesis.

claim: For pairs of recording sites with category-selective beta synchrony, no synchrony was detected between parietal spikes with prefrontal oscillations.
source: By contrast, for pairs of recording sites with category-selective beta synchrony, we did not detect any synchrony between parietal spikes with prefrontal oscillations.
evidence: This reports a negative finding that supports the directionality interpretation.

claim: The findings suggest a top-down influence from the PFC to parietal cortex.
source: This all suggests a top-down influence from the PFC to parietal cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the asymmetric synchrony findings.

claim: The results are in line with other studies that indicate prefrontal and parietal cortex involvement in visual categorization.
source: Our results are in line with other studies that indicate prefrontal and parietal cortex involvement in visual categorization (Braunlich et al., 2015; Crowe et al., 2013; Goodwin et al., 2012; Swaminathan and Freedman, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neurons in both PFC and PPC show correlates of a variety of abstract cognitive factors such as number, shape and spatial categories.
source: Neurons in both areas show correlates of a variety of abstract cognitive factors such as number, shape and spatial categories (Goodwin et al., 2012; Murata et al., 2000; Tudusciuc and Nieder, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Chafee and colleagues and Merchant and colleagues have previously reported single-neuron correlates of spatial categories.
source: Chafee and colleagues and Merchant and colleagues have previously reported single-neuron correlates of spatial categories.
evidence: This references prior research on spatial categorization.

claim: By analyzing the fluctuations of the time course of spiking from both PFC and PPC, previous researchers concluded that category information was transmitted in a top-down fashion from the PFC to parietal cortex.
source: By analyzing the fluctuations of the time course of spiking from both areas, they also concluded that category information was transmitted in a top-down fashion from the PFC to parietal cortex (Crowe et al., 2013; Merchant et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The spatial categories may be computed in prefrontal circuits, where this information intermingles with bottom-up information (the task-irrelevant distinction between the hemifields).
source: In sum, our results suggest that the spatial categories may be computed in prefrontal circuits, where this information intermingles with bottom-up information (in this case, the task-irrelevant distinction between the hemifields).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about where category information is computed.

claim: The prefrontal cortex selectively broadcasts via beta rhythms, and thus strengthens, only the relevant information back to the parietal cortex.
source: But the prefrontal cortex selectively broadcasts via beta rhythms, and thus strengthens, only the relevant information back to the parietal cortex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of selective information transmission.

claim: Long-range frontoparietal networks supported by synchronized beta rhythms permit the most relevant representation to dominate and guide the animal's category decision.
source: Long-range frontoparietal networks supported by synchronized beta rhythms, then, permit the most relevant representation to dominate and guide the animal's category decision.
evidence: This is the main conclusion about the functional role of beta synchrony in categorization.

claim: Data were collected from two adult male rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta), weighing 10–12 kg.
source: Data were collected from two adult male rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta), weighing 10–12 kg.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: The animals were taken care of in accordance with the National Institutes of Health guidelines and the policies of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Committee for Animal Care.
source: The animals were taken care of in accordance with the National Institutes of Health guidelines and the policies of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Committee for Animal Care.
evidence: This describes the ethical oversight of the animal research.

claim: Both animals were trained on the rule-based categorization task until they reached similar levels of proficiency.
source: Both animals were trained on the rule-based categorization task until they reached similar levels of proficiency.
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: Each animal was surgically implanted with one titanium headbolt and two titanium recording chambers.
source: Each of them was surgically implanted with one titanium headbolt and two titanium recording chambers, one of which was placed above the left principal sulcus and the other above the left intraparietal sulcus.
evidence: This describes the surgical preparation for recordings.

claim: Placement of the chambers and estimation of the electrode recording sites were guided by structural MRI scans and computed with Matlab.
source: Placement of the chambers as well as estimation of the electrode recording sites were guided by structural MRI scans and computed with Matlab (Mathworks, Natick MA).
evidence: This describes the method for localizing recording sites.

claim: Neural data were collected from 39 experiments (22 experiments from animal G and 17 from animal P).
source: Neural data were collected from 39 experiments (22 experiments from animal G and 17 from animal P).
evidence: This reports the number of recording sessions.
